result:
I'd like to write about lichen, because almost no one does, and it deserves better.

Lichen is not one thing. It's a fungus that has taken in a partner—an alga, or a cyanobacterium, sometimes both, and in many species a yeast that nobody noticed until 2016—and built a body around it. The fungus provides structure and shelter and mineral scavenging; the alga does the photosynthesizing and pays rent in sugar. For a long time biologists argued about whether to call this symbiosis or controlled captivity, and I think the honest answer is that the question is ours, not the lichen's. The arrangement has worked for hundreds of millions of years. It was there when the first plants were still figuring out how to stand up.

What I find quietly astonishing is the pace. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*—the one that looks like a shattered yellow-green mosaic on granite—grows perhaps half a millimeter a year. Some individual patches are thought to be several thousand years old. Geologists use them as clocks: measure the largest lichen on a boulder and you can estimate when the glacier dropped it there. A living thing, used as a calendar for stone.

And they are the first to arrive anywhere hard. Bare rock, a fresh lava field, a gravestone, the roof tile you never look at. They secrete weak acids and slowly, over centuries, take the rock apart, and when they die they leave behind the first thin smear of soil that a moss can grip, and then a grass, and then everything else. Every forest is standing on a foundation lichen prepared and got no credit for.

They've been to space, too. Samples strapped to the outside of the International Space Station for a year and a half—vacuum, radiation, temperature swings of hundreds of degrees—came back and resumed photosynthesizing as if they'd been napping.

I like lichen because it's a rebuke to a lot of the stories we tell about what life is supposed to look like. It isn't fast. It isn't individual. It isn't clearly one organism or two or three. It doesn't compete so much as persist. It is what happens when several things that could not survive alone decide, without deciding, to become a surface together and wait.

There's a patch of it on nearly every rock you've ever sat on. It was there before you and it will still be there, a few millimeters wider, long after. I find that oddly comforting—not that it outlasts us, but that something so unhurried and so unbothered is doing its slow work on every exposed face of the world, and needs nothing from us at all, and is beautiful anyway, in a way you only see once you stop and look at what you assumed was just a stain.
